analysis.one_liner: Requires mammography facilities to be federally certified, with quality standards, annual inspections, and public reporting of violations.
analysis.headline: Backed by 63 senators and approved by the Senate committee, the bill was placed on the Senate calendar on October 1, 1992 and never brought to a floor vote before Congress ended — though equivalent standards were signed into law weeks later.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required every hospital, clinic, radiology practice, and mobile unit that performs mammograms to obtain a federal certificate. To keep it, a facility would have to use dedicated mammography equipment, employ trained and certified staff, pass annual inspections by qualified physicists, and keep quality-control records. Facilities that failed would face fines, suspension, or shutdown, and the government would publish an annual public list of violators. Medicare would only pay for mammograms done at certified facilities.
analysis.who_benefits: Women getting mammograms, whose screening images would come from certified equipment read by certified physicians under enforced quality standards. The bill also ties Medicare payment to certification, so the federal program would only fund facilities that meet the standards, and directs grants for training health workers in breast cancer prevention.

how_it_helps.text: No facility could legally perform or interpret mammograms without a federal certificate, with standards covering equipment, personnel training, and quality assurance [S2][S3][S4].

The Secretary of Health and Human Services would inspect every certified facility at least annually, checking image quality and radiation dose, and could fine facilities up to $10,000 per violation, suspend or revoke certificates, and sue to shut down facilities posing a health hazard [S2][S4].

Each year the Secretary would publish a public list of facilities convicted of fraud or kickbacks, sanctioned, or stripped of their certificates, with reasons — giving patients information about where to go [S2][S3][S4].
Medicare would be required to pay for screening mammograms only when performed at a certified facility meeting the new standards [S2][S4].

analysis.who_pays: Mammography facilities — hospitals, clinics, radiology practices, and mobile units — bear the compliance costs: certificate and inspection fees designed to cover the program's costs, dedicated mammography equipment, certified personnel and physicists, and recordkeeping. Some of that cost would likely flow to patients and insurers through higher prices, and federal grant programs would cost taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: Facilities would pay certificate and inspection fees set to cover the program's full administration costs, plus the cost of dedicated equipment and annual physicist inspections — expenses that could be passed on to patients and would weigh heaviest on small practices and mobile units [S4].

Requiring physicians to be board-certified to read mammograms and staff to be licensed or certified could shrink the pool of people allowed to provide screening, raising access concerns in rural areas, and the committee version softened inspections to allow 48 hours' notice during regular business hours rather than unannounced checks [S3][S4].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits — more reliable breast cancer detection at a moment when the reliability of mammography was in question — are large and broadly shared. The costs are real but conventional for a health-regulation program: fees and equipment standards borne by providers and passed partly to patients. The committee's softening of inspections (48 hours' notice) weakened enforcement somewhat, but the core certification, inspection, penalty, and public-reporting structure survived into the reported version.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate committee approved the bill and put it on the Senate calendar on October 1, 1992, but the Senate never voted on it before the Congress ended on January 3, 1993.

narrative.text: Introduced October 1, 1991 by Sen. Brock Adams, joined by Sens. Barbara Mikulski and Dave Durenberger, and referred to the Labor and Human Resources Committee [S4][S6].
The bill drew 63 cosponsors — 44 Democrats and 19 Republicans — within its first months [S5].
The committee held hearings in October 1991, ordered the bill reported favorably in September 1992, and reported it with an amendment on October 1, 1992, with additional views filed [S6].
The reported version softened the original inspection scheme, requiring 48 hours' notice of inspections, subject to waiver, during regular hours of operation [S3].
The bill was placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on October 1, 1992, and no further action was taken before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993 [S6].

Weeks before this Congress ended, Congress passed and President George H.W. Bush signed the Mammography Quality Standards Act of 1992, Public Law 102-539, establishing federal certification and inspection of mammography facilities — the same core protections this bill contained.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: In the short run, mammography facilities gained a few extra months without certification fees and compliance costs. But the advantage was temporary: the same standards became law weeks later through another bill, so the public did not ultimately lose the protections.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Facilities briefly — then the law passed anyway

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines heavily: of 63 cosponsors, 44 were Democrats and 19 Republicans, and both parties' members appeared among the original sponsors; no member is recorded opposing it.

industries.industry: Mammography facilities (hospitals, radiology practices, clinics, mobile units)
industries.note: The bill imposes certification, annual inspections, fees covering program costs, civil penalties up to $10,000, and public listing of violators on these providers. Their regulatory burden is the direct counterpart of the safety and accuracy benefits patients receive.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit accreditation bodies (such as radiology professional organizations)
industries.note: The bill makes Secretary-approved private nonprofit accreditors the official channel for certifying mammography facilities, giving them a permanent government-backed role in deciding which facilities may operate. Their continued approval depends on applying standards at least as strict as the federal ones, so their gatekeeping role runs alongside patient safety.

Quality standards would require facilities to use radiological equipment specifically designed for mammography, forcing providers to buy dedicated machines and pay for annual physicist inspections. That is a sales benefit for manufacturers, with costs passed to facilities and patients.
